images.alt: A matt black Sinclair ZX81 with its membrane keyboard, photographed from the front
images.caption: The ZX81, launched in March 1981, folded the ZX80's twenty-one chips down to four inside Jim Westwood's redesign.
images.author: AUIC Oficial

images.alt: A Sinclair ZX81 on display in a computer museum, shown from the front with its printed membrane keyboard
images.caption: Rick Dickinson's wedge-shaped case and flat membrane keyboard replaced moving keys entirely, to hold the kit price at £49.95.
images.author: MKFI

images.alt: A Sinclair ZX81 computer viewed at a three-quarter angle, showing its black wedge case and rear edge connector
images.caption: Every keyword on the membrane is a single keystroke, because the machine's one kilobyte of memory has no room to spare for spelling them out.
images.author: MOS6502

images.alt: A Sinclair ZX81 with its 16 KB RAM pack plugged into the rear edge connector, on display at a retrocomputing event
images.caption: The 16 KB RAM pack turned the ZX81 into a machine you could write a real program on — and was notorious for working loose and losing an evening's typing.
images.author: Soupmeister

images.alt: A Sinclair ZX81 computer photographed close up, showing the keyword labels printed on each key of the membrane keyboard
images.caption: Three or four BASIC keywords are printed on every key, because Sinclair BASIC never expects you to type one out letter by letter.
images.author: babbagecabbage
